title: Amortized Analysis
description: Understand amortized analysis for operations that have occasional high costs

blocks.text: Till now, we've been looking at algorithms using Worst-Case Analysis. We pick one operation and ask
"What's the maximum work this operation can ever do?"
That's the Big O we've been calculating. It's useful. But sometimes, it makes a fast algorithm look slow.
Here's a classic example:

Think about a Stack a simple data structure where you push and pop items. Most of the time, pushing an item is super fast O(1). But sometimes, when the stack runs out of space, it has to resize itself, and that takes longer. During resizing:
This copying takes O(n) time. So what's the actual cost of a push? Is it O(1) or O(n)? That's exactly what Amortized Analysis helps us figure out.
In many algorithms, most operations are cheap, but a few are expensive.
If we only look at the worst single operation, the algorithm looks bad. But if we zoom out and look at many operations together, the picture changes completely.
Amortized Analysis says:
"Don't judge one operation. Look at the average cost across many operations."
Simple Real Life Example
Imagine you go to a cricket stadium.

items: Buying a single match ticket costs ₹500 each time.
But if you buy a season pass for ₹5000, you can watch all 20 matches for "free" after that.

blocks.text: If someone asks "How much does one match cost you?"

items: Worst case: ₹5000 (the day you bought the pass).

blocks.text: But neither is the real answer. The fair answer is:
₹5000 ÷ 20 matches = ₹250 per match that's the amortized cost.
Amortized Analysis does the same thing for algorithms. It spreads the cost of expensive operations across all the cheap ones.
Amortized vs. Average vs. Worst Case
People often confuse these three. Here's a simple breakdown:
The key difference: Amortized analysis doesn't care about random inputs. It just looks at how the algorithm behaves over a long run.
Let's take a stack that starts with space for 4 items.
You push items one by one:

codes.javascript:
Push A → [A, _, _, _]   cost: 1
Push B → [A, B, _, _]   cost: 1
Push C → [A, B, C, _]   cost: 1
Push D → [A, B, C, D]   cost: 1

blocks.text: Stack is full. Now you push E:
The Expensive Step happens:

items: A new stack with double the space (capacity = 8) is created.
All 4 old items (A, B, C, D) are copied over.
E is added at the end.

codes.javascript: [A, B, C, D, E, _, _, _]   cost: 4 copies + 1 write = 5

blocks.text: That one push costO(N). But the next few pushes are cheap again:

codes.javascript:
Push F → cost: 1
Push G → cost: 1
Push H → cost: 1

blocks.text: Now let's count the total cost for 8 pushes:
Simple pushes: 7 × 1 = 7 One expensive resize: 5 Total = 12 operations for 8 pushes → average ≈ 1.5 per push
Even with the expensive resize, the average cost per push stays close to O(1).
Amortized cost per push = O(1)
Mathematicians have three standard methods to do this analysis properly:
1. Aggregate Method (Simplest)
Add up the total cost of all operations, then divide by the number of operations.
Stack example:

items: n pushes cost O(n) total → amortized cost = O(n)/n = O(1) per push

blocks.text: 2. Accounting Method (Token/Credit approach)
Give each operation some "extra credits" upfront.
Stack example:

items: Charge every push 3 credits:1 credit → for the actual push2 credits → saved for future resizing
When resize happens, saved credits pay for the copying.

blocks.text: 3. Potential Method (Most formal)
Think of the data structure as having "stored energy" called potential (Φ).
Formula:
Amortized cost = Actual cost + (Φ after − Φ before)
When energy builds up, it pays for future expensive operations. This method is used in advanced topics like Fibonacci Heaps and Union-Find.

blocks.text: What's Next?
Now we understand how to handle algorithms where some operations are cheap and some are expensive.
But what about recursive algorithms like Merge Sort or Binary Search where the problem keeps breaking itself into smaller pieces?
For those, we need a different tool called a Recurrence Relation. We'll explore that in the next chapter
